blocks.text: Preference optimization is the umbrella term for the family of techniques, RLHF, DPO, ORPO, KTO, and constitutional AI, all covered in earlier topics of this module, that share a common goal, adjusting a model behavior to better match human preferences rather than just imitating labeled examples the way supervised fine-tuning does.
This topic steps back from any single method to compare the family as a whole, giving a practical framework for choosing among them based on the data, compute, and quality tradeoffs each one makes.
1. What Preference Optimization Means

blocks.alt: RLHF, DPO, ORPO, KTO, and Constitutional AI all belong to the preference optimization family

blocks.text: Preference optimization refers broadly to any training approach that uses signals about which responses are preferred, whether from human labelers, reward models, or a model applying written principles, rather than relying only on a single correct target the way standard supervised fine-tuning, covered earlier in this course, does.
2. The Common Goal Across Methods

blocks.alt: A base model output is optimized toward being aligned with human preferences

blocks.text: Every method covered in this module, despite differing mechanics, pursues the same underlying goal, shifting a model output distribution so that responses humans would prefer become more likely and responses humans would reject become less likely, without simply memorizing a fixed set of target outputs.
3. Reward Model Based vs Direct Methods

blocks.alt: Reward model based RLHF is compared against direct methods like DPO, ORPO, and KTO

blocks.text: RLHF, covered in an earlier topic, trains a separate reward model, then uses reinforcement learning, typically PPO, also covered earlier, to optimize against it, DPO, ORPO, and KTO instead optimize directly on preference data without ever training a standalone reward model, a structural split that shapes most of the other tradeoffs in this comparison.
4. Comparing Data Requirements

blocks.alt: Paired preference data is compared against unpaired label data

blocks.text: RLHF, DPO, and ORPO all typically need paired preference data, a chosen and a rejected response for the same prompt, KTO, covered in an earlier topic, is the outlier here, working directly with unpaired, individually labeled desirable or undesirable examples, a real practical advantage when paired data is hard to collect.
5. Comparing Training Complexity and Stability

blocks.alt: Simple, stable training is compared against complex, higher ceiling training

blocks.text: DPO and ORPO are generally simpler to train and more stable than full RLHF, since they skip the separate reward model and reinforcement learning loop, RLHF, in exchange for that added complexity, has historically shown a higher ceiling on some tasks when tuned carefully, a tradeoff between ease of use and maximum achievable quality.

blocks.text: 6. Comparing Compute Cost

RLHF and constitutional AI both tend to cost more compute overall, RLHF because it trains and runs a separate reward model alongside reinforcement learning, constitutional AI because its self critique and revision process, covered in the previous topic, requires extra generation passes, DPO, ORPO, and KTO are generally cheaper since they skip these extra components.
7. A Practical Decision Framework

blocks.alt: The data available drives a choice between DPO, KTO, or RLHF

blocks.text: A practical starting point is to look at what data is already available, clean paired preference data points toward DPO, existing unpaired feedback signals like thumbs up or down point toward KTO, and a need to squeeze out maximum quality with a larger compute budget points toward RLHF, with constitutional AI worth considering specifically when scaling human labeling effort is the binding constraint.

blocks.title: There is no universally best method
blocks.content: Published comparisons across these methods show results that vary meaningfully by task and dataset, the practical decision usually comes down to available data shape and compute budget more than any method being categorically superior.

blocks.text: 8. Combining Methods in Practice

These methods are not always mutually exclusive, a pipeline might use constitutional AI style self critique to generate preference data cheaply, then train with DPO on the resulting pairs, or use RLHF for a first pass and a lighter method like ORPO for subsequent refinement rounds, combining the strengths of more than one approach.
9. Where This Fits in the Overall Pipeline

blocks.alt: An SFT stage is followed by a preference optimization stage, producing a deployed aligned model

blocks.text: Regardless of which specific method is chosen, preference optimization typically runs as a stage after supervised fine-tuning, covered earlier in this course, refining a model that already follows instructions reasonably well into one whose responses better match nuanced human preferences before it reaches production.
Worked Example

A team building an internal coding assistant already has a supervised fine-tuned model. They have some paired preference data from earlier evaluation work, along with a much larger pool of unpaired thumbs up and down feedback collected from production usage.

Rather than picking one method exclusively, they run an initial DPO pass on the paired data, then continue refining with KTO on the larger unpaired feedback pool, using each method where its data requirements are the best fit rather than forcing all their data into a single method shape.
Common Mistakes

items: Assuming one method, usually RLHF, is always the best choice regardless of available data or compute budget
Ignoring existing unpaired feedback data that KTO could use directly, in favor of an expensive new paired data collection effort
Treating preference optimization methods as mutually exclusive when a pipeline can combine more than one
Skipping supervised fine-tuning entirely and expecting preference optimization alone to teach a model basic task competence

blocks.text: Practice

For a fine-tuning project you are familiar with or could imagine, list what preference data, paired or unpaired, is realistically available, then use the decision framework in this topic to choose which method from this module you would start with and explain why.
Key Takeaway

Preference optimization is a family of methods, RLHF, DPO, ORPO, KTO, and constitutional AI, that all share the same goal of aligning model behavior with human preferences, and the right choice among them comes down mostly to what data shape is available and how much compute and training complexity a team is willing to take on, not any single method being universally best.
